item.title: Int'l expeditions in China unlock secrets of Asia's longest cave
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-04
GUIYANG, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- For French caver Jean Bottazzi, caves never disappoint. In the vast underground maze of Shuanghe Cave in southwest China's Guizhou Province, even an unfinished mission can lead to an unexpected discovery, opening up whole new horizons. Bottazzi has spent more than two decades exploring Shuanghe, witnessing its 25-year journey of international exploration. Situated in Suiyang County, it is the world's third-longest cave system and Asia's longest. Since the first China-France joint exploration in 2001, the mapped cave system has expanded from several dozen kilometers of known passages to more than 480 kilometers. The latest findings from the 25th international cave scientific expedition were announced last month in Suiyang. Another 41.8 kilometers were added to the mapped passages. With the newly added length, the cave system now stretches 481.5 kilometers and reaches a vertical depth of 912 meters. It has 124 interconnected entrances. For Bottazzi, as well as the scientists and explorers who have worked alongside him, the significance of Shuanghe Cave cannot be measured by its length alone. It is also a vast natural archive that preserves clues to the evolution of species, the changing climate and the geological history of southwest China. Researchers found nine additional individual giant panda fossils, mostly in newly explored passages, during the 25th international expedition this year, bringing the total number of individual giant panda fossils discovered in Shuanghe Cave to 61. They also found two sites bearing clear giant panda claw marks. Wang Deyuan, an associate research fellow at the Guizhou Academy of Sciences' Institute of Mountain Resources, said the marks and the structure of the cave passages offer clues to how some of the animals may have died. The pandas apparently entered the cave and moved more than 10 meters inward before falling into a vertical shaft. They survived the initial fall and left claw marks as they tried to move on, but eventually fell into a deeper shaft and became trapped, Wang said. The latest expedition also uncovered fossils of ancient animals. Among them, fossils of a giant tapir and a clouded leopard were found in Shuanghe Cave for the first time. For Bottazzi, however, the fascination of cave exploration lies not only in what researchers find, but also in what they do not expect to find. A recent expedition experience reminded Bottazzi once again why he fell in love with caves in the first place. The team had set out to connect several caves at the northern end of the Shuanghe Cave system, but the goal remained elusive. However, the story didn't end there. As they groped their way forward, something entirely unexpected appeared before them -- an entire magnificent wall of gypsum crystals. "Curiosity instantly rekindled a new thrill of exploration and unexpectedly opened up a new direction," Bottazzi recalled. "If we had focused only on our planned goal, we would never have met this surprise. Half disappointment, half satisfaction -- that is the true charm of cave exploration," he said. The Shuanghe Cave also serves as an archive with hidden clues to ancient climate. Researchers have been conducting uranium-series dating of calcite deposits inside the cave, according to Bottazzi. "As long as we can find calcite samples of different ages and combine them with isotope analysis, we can obtain a record of climate evolution from the present day all the way back a million years," Bottazzi said. "It is an extremely precious archive of paleoclimate." The line of research made a breakthrough this year. Using the new uranium-lead isotope dating technique, the research team determined that some secondary carbonate deposits inside the cave are more than five million years old. The finding significantly extends the chronological framework for the development of Shuanghe Cave and other large caves in the karst regions of southwest China. The vast underground maze of Shuanghe Cave has not only yielded a string of discoveries that have captivated the scientific world, but also become a vivid example of international cooperation in cave research. Asked how Chinese and foreign researchers share exploration data and cave maps, Bottazzi was unequivocal: "We work for science. All the data and cave maps are shared." For Bottazzi, the cave has continued to captivate him so deeply that in recent years he settled in Shuanghe Village in Wenquan Township, Suiyang. Over the years, he has become such a familiar face in the village that locals affectionately call him "Lao Rang," or "Old Jean." To Bottazzi, there are few better places than Shuanghe to explore the Earth's hidden treasures. The cave is a world of diverse landscapes, from underground rivers and vast chambers draped with waterfalls to completely dry fossil galleries. "We are exploring as if inside a maze; you can never guess where the passage leads, and you have to keep thinking. For cave exploration, this is a wonderfully fascinating place," Bottazzi said. ■

item.title: China's cat parks seek lasting, sustainable homes for strays
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-04
Cats are seen at Chongqing Firefly Bay Cat Harbor Park in Chongqing, southwest China, Oct. 4, 2026. (Xinhua/Wu Yanxia) CHONGQING/HARBIN, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- When Chongqing Firefly Bay Cat Harbor Park opened on New Year's Day in southwest China, it had just over 600 cats. More than eight months later, the number has passed 1,000. By September, the 30,000-square-meter riverside park had rescued or taken in more than 1,300 cats, while over 240 had been adopted. As the number of cats grows, so do the demands on the park -- from veterinary care and staffing to finding enough space for new arrivals. "The first thing is to keep the daily operation running," said Jian Ning, who oversees offline operations at the park. "We have to survive first before talking about anything else." The park sits on what was a long-idle site near Nanbin Road in Chongqing Municipality. The local government provides the land rent-free, while the operator earns revenue from admission fees, spending inside the park and rent paid by businesses on the site. A ticket costs 19.9 yuan (about 3 U.S. dollars). During the city's hot summer, when fewer people visit the outdoor park, daily attendance averages just over 300. On its busiest day, however, the park received 8,000 visitors. Veterinary care accounts for roughly one-third of operating costs, Jian said. Current revenue is enough to keep the park running day to day, but making a profit remains difficult. "If we had to pay normal rent, the operating pressure would be much greater," Jian said. The park now employs 51 people, including animal-care staff, security guards and cleaners. Most employees who work directly with the cats are in their 20s. All are paid, full-time staff. "We don't expect people to work simply for love," Jian said. Most members of the park's core team are from stray-cat rescue groups. They had seen rescue efforts struggle with a basic problem: expenses kept mounting, while funding often depended on donations, subsidies or rescuers paying out of their own pockets. The team therefore decided to open the site to visitors, hoping revenue from ticket sales and other businesses could help cover the cost of long-term care for rescued cats. The park sums up the idea in a lighthearted slogan: "Cats work to support themselves." The experiment is unfolding alongside a sizable pet economy. China had 126 million pet dogs and cats in urban areas in 2025, including 72.89 million cats, while the urban dog-and-cat consumer market reached 312.6 billion yuan, according to the 2026 China Pet Industry White Paper (Consumption Report). Yet space has a limit. Jian estimated that the park could accommodate 2,000 to 3,000 cats. If the population approaches that level, she said, new admissions will have to be reduced. The park does not encourage people to relocate stray cats that are regularly fed in residential communities, as they have already grown accustomed to those surroundings, Jian said. Scientific research also suggests that managing free-roaming cat populations requires more than one-off interventions. A 12-year controlled study published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences found that sustained, high-intensity neutering across contiguous areas could reduce cat numbers, while immigration and other compensatory effects could weaken the impact. The researchers recommended combining the trap-neuter-return method with complementary measures such as adoption and resource management. Adoption certainly provides another outlet. Applicants face strict requirements, however, and the park conducts follow-up checks. None of the more than 240 adopted cats have so far been returned. Visitors, meanwhile, must adapt to rules designed around the animals. Children under six are not admitted, and staff ask visitors not to chase cats or pick them up against their will. Jian said disputes over scratches and bites have become less common as visitor guidance has improved. The park may stop admitting visitors once more than 3,000 people are inside. So far, the flow of people in and out has made that unnecessary. Some 3,000 kilometers away in northeast China, another cat park is testing a similar combination of animal rescue and tourism on a smaller scale. Scarlett's Friends, Heilongjiang Province's first cat-themed park, opened on Aug. 28 at the Yabuli Ski Resort in Harbin and is now home to 150 rescued stray cats. The cat park occupies a site that had stood idle for years and gives Yabuli, long known for winter skiing, another attraction for the warmer months. Before entering areas open to visitors, the cats must be neutered, vaccinated, treated for parasites, and assessed to determine whether they can adapt to interaction with people. Sick cats are moved to an isolation area, while a partner veterinary hospital provides regular health support. Winter in Yabuli brings temperatures far below freezing. Indoor activity areas and cat houses have been equipped with air-source heating systems, and the cats will spend most of the winter indoors, said Liu Guangpeng, deputy general manager of Harbin Yabuli Tourism Investment Group Co., Ltd. Ning Xiaofeng, general manager of the group, said stray-cat rescue that relies solely on continued spending is difficult to sustain. By linking the park with tourism, the operator aims to use tourism revenue to help cover the cost of caring for the cats while providing them with a stable home. Liu said the park would limit visitor numbers rather than compromise the cats' welfare. "Even if there were no visitors, we would still make sure the cats were properly cared for," he said. If crowds exceeded the park's capacity, it would introduce reservations and limit entry. Similar ideas have begun to appear in local policies. In February, the eastern Chinese city of Nanjing in Jiangsu Province issued guidelines encouraging pet-related tourism while calling for stray animals to be managed via capture, neutering, return or adoption. The document also said eligible animal-protection groups could receive support through government service purchases and public-interest programs. Back in Chongqing, Jian explained that relying entirely on subsidies, donations or unpaid work would not be sustainable. "Only by using commercial operations to support rescue can we keep this going in the long run," she said. During Chongqing's hot summer, the park stays open until midnight. As temperatures fall in the evening, visitors arrive to see the cats and enjoy the riverside night view. Many simply sit and wait. "Here, you don't have to talk or please anyone," Jian said. "You can just sit on the steps, and maybe a cat will come over, rub against you or fall asleep in your lap." ■ Tourists interact with cats at Chongqing Firefly Bay Cat Harbor Park in Chongqing, southwest China, Oct. 4, 2026. item.title: From import replacement to global exporter, Chinese harvester maker sweetens sugarcane business
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-04
by Xinhua writer Zhang Yunlong ZHENGZHOU, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- "People say a woman fears marrying the wrong man, while a man fears choosing the wrong trade. I definitely chose the wrong trade," Zhang Changxian, 59, said with a laugh. When Zhang began developing a sugarcane harvester in 2008, he expected challenges. He did not expect it would take eight years to bring the machine to market. For years, the engineer-turned-entrepreneur and his team spent harvest seasons testing and redesigning prototypes in cane fields in Chongzuo, south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region. The city is about 1,600 km from his factory in Luoyang, central China's Henan Province. During one field test, a steering linkage snapped in a muddy patch. In many others, the machine struggled with cane flattened by typhoons. Today, machines made by his company, Luoyang Chenhan Agricultural Equipment Technology, account for about half of China's sugarcane harvester market by volume, the company says. They are also drawing buyers overseas, from Southeast Asia to Latin America. The company's rise comes as China's sugar industry seeks to cut costs and improve competitiveness through mechanization. China has long relied on imports to bridge a wide gap between domestic sugar output and demand. In the 2024/25 marketing year, the country produced about 11.2 million tonnes of sugar and consumed about 15.7 million tonnes, according to the Chinese Agriculture Outlook Committee under the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs. Imports totaled about 4.6 million tonnes. According to Zhang, major sugar-exporting countries such as Brazil generally enjoy lower production costs, with large-scale mechanized farming being one of the key factors. Rising labor costs have added to the pressure on China's sugar industry. When Zhang entered the industry in 2008, a worker could harvest about one tonne of cane a day for 25 to 30 yuan (3.7 to 4.5 U.S. dollars). Today, the same work can cost 180 to 250 yuan, he said, while harvested cane sells for around 500 yuan a tonne. As labor costs climb, demand for mechanized harvesting has grown. One Chenhan harvester, Zhang said, can now cut more than 100 tonnes of cane a day, roughly the work of 100 laborers. When Zhang started, nearly all harvesters in China were imported. His team decided to develop equipment tailored to local conditions. But building a domestic harvester proved far harder than many had expected. Unlike in Brazil and Australia, where cane is often grown on large plantations, China's major sugarcane regions typically have sloping terrain, with smaller and more fragmented fields. Many major agricultural machinery makers focused on larger markets for wheat, corn and rice equipment, while sugarcane harvesting was a niche segment with significant technical challenges. With no established supply chains or mature domestic components for sugarcane harvesters at the time, Zhang's team had to design and test many critical systems themselves. Each year offered only a narrow testing window because cane is harvested in a specific season, so a design flaw found in the field often meant waiting another year for large-scale trials. After nearly three years without a breakthrough, Zhang put the project on hold for a while. Experts, including his former mentor, advised him to give up, he recalled. A turning point came in 2011 when the team resumed work and shifted from an earlier whole-stalk harvesting approach to a chopped-cane system better suited to Chinese field conditions. "At times we nearly ran out of money," Zhang said. To keep going, he used money set aside for his daughter's education and later mortgaged property to fund development. Chenhan completed its first harvester in 2015. The machine entered the market a year later and sold more than 30 units in 2016, rising to more than 150 the following year. Overseas expansion began in 2019. The company has since exported machines to countries including Vietnam, Thailand, Indonesia, Costa Rica and Venezuela. Exports account for about one-fifth of revenue and are growing steadily, Zhang said. Many foreign buyers are drawn by lower prices and the company's willingness to customize equipment. Customers in the French overseas department of Reunion, for example, requested tracked harvesters able to work on volcanic soil. The company developed a specialized tracked machine to reduce ground pressure and optimized its cooling systems for the island's tropical climate. Looking ahead, Zhang said the company is exploring smarter controls, hybrid power systems and lower fuel consumption. "Many people told us Chinese companies couldn't make a sugarcane harvester," Zhang said, recalling the early doubts. "We made it, and now we're exporting it." ■

item.title: Xinhua Headlines: China's new generation shines at Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-04
* China reaffirmed its continental dominance by topping the gold medal table for a record 12th straight Asian Games, securing 169 gold, 89 silver and 83 bronze medals - its best-ever haul at an overseas Asiad. * The Games signaled a changing of the guard, with 548 of China's 815 athletes making their Asiad debuts and over a quarter born in 2005 or later. * Beyond traditional disciplines, young Chinese athletes broke new ground in skateboarding, sport climbing, surfing and BMX freestyle-sports aligned with the Olympic program's youth-oriented shift. NAGOYA, Japan, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- The Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games came to a close Sunday, with China topping the gold medal table for the 12th consecutive edition, and finishing with 169 gold, 89 silver and 83 bronze medals, its best haul at an overseas Asiad. Beyond the medal count, the Games offered a glimpse of the next generation of Chinese athletes. Young competitors rose up across a spectrum of sports -- strengthening China's traditional powerhouses, breaking new ground in emerging disciplines and signaling ambitions that extend well beyond Nagoya. DEPTH ON DISPLAY China's dominance in its traditional strength events was evident throughout the Games. Diving once again provided the clearest example. With Lian Junjie winning the men's 10m platform title, China swept all 10 diving gold medals on offer at the Games. Since making its Asiad debut in 1974, China has never missed out on a diving gold medal, and the latest title was the team's 100th diving gold in Asian Games history. That dominance extended across the water. Chinese swimmers won 30 gold, 13 silver and 11 bronze medals, their best-ever haul at the Games. They also swept all seven relay titles for the first time, while setting five Asian records and 17 Games records. On the track and field, China continued to turn depth into medals. The team won 17 gold, 14 silver and eight bronze medals, its best show at an Asiad held outside China since Bangkok 1998, to finish atop the athletics medal table. The momentum also extended to other medal-rich events. China claimed 16 of the overall 28 shooting titles and set five world records. "The Asiad gave us an opportunity to test our preparations for Los Angeles 2028," said Wang Lian, an official with China's shooting and archery administration. "It was also an important step in developing our team, particularly our promising young athletes." Weightlifting and gymnastics further underscored China's strength in established events. Yang Liuyue broke world records in the snatch and total in the women's 61kg category, while the men's gymnastics team captured its 13th consecutive Games title and the women's team extended its winning streak to 14 editions. YOUTH TAKES FLIGHT China's delegation had a distinctly youthful look at the Asiad. Of its 815 athletes, 548 were making their Asian Games debuts, while 27 percent were born in 2005 or later. In the women's 400m individual medley, 13-year-old Yu Zidi and 15-year-old Ke Wenxi took gold and silver. Yu won three golds, setting Asian Games records in the 200m butterfly and 400m individual medley, as well as an Asian record in the 200m individual medley. Her performances earned her the women's Most Valuable Player award, announced by the Olympic Council of Asia on Sunday. They arrived with talent, but talent alone was not enough. Behind their breakthroughs were years of repetition, training and persistence. "Only I know how much I went through this year. But I got through it all. I hope I can keep getting better and better," Yu said. 19-year-old Zhang Zhanshuo won seven gold medals, the most of any athlete at the Games. His celebration of counting the golds on his fingers in the pool became one of the memorable images. That confidence was on display in the field, too. 18-year-old javelin thrower Yan Ziyi made an immediate impact, launching 70.46 meters with her first attempt to improve the Games record by 4.37 meters. "I plan to save my chance to break the world record for the 2027 World Championships in Beijing," Yan said. The emergence of young athletes such as teenage sprinter Chen Yujie offers a glimpse of what could lie ahead for Asian athletics. The 17-year-old competed in four events and won three golds and a silver, including a gold in the women's 100m in a Games-record 11.06 seconds. Off the track, her confidence was just as striking. A photo that she took a nap in the athletes' lounge before the final became a hit on Chinese social media. "These Asian Games have given me a lot of motivation. Now that it's over, I'm already looking ahead to the next challenge," Chen said. "I hope that one day I can represent China and Asian women on the world stage and showcase our strength at the Olympics." BREAKING NEW GROUND Young athletes are opening up new possibilities for Chinese sports. After years of struggling to regain the footing, China's men's football team beat Uzbekistan in a penalty shootout on Saturday to win a bronze medal, its first in 28 years at the Games. The result gave Chinese fans something more to celebrate during the National Day holiday. "This is the most valuable medal of my career," said 21-year-old center back Peng Xiao. "But I would rather see it as a starting point. I hope the generation that comes after us can one day stand higher on the podium." As the Olympic program embraces younger, more urban sports, skateboarding, sport climbing, surfing and BMX freestyle have become regular features at the Asian Games. Chinese athletes are making their mark in these events, chasing results while gaining recognition on the world stage. China's climbers made their presence felt on National Day, sweeping the women's boulder and men's speed titles to claim the country's first Asian Games gold medals in Olympic events. With Olympic and world champions in the field, both victories were hard-earned. For 17-year-old Yang Siqi, reaching the Asiad surfing final and winning women's shortboard silver turned what once seemed out of reach into reality. The teenager from the mountainous region of southwestern China secured the country's first Asian Games surfing medal. Her dedication in training even caught the attention of Song Min, a coach with South Korea's surfing team, who said he believed Yang could one day make it to the Olympics. "I have never been afraid of surfing since I first started," Yang said. "The next step is to keep improving, one step at a time." China's skateboarders also came out on top against the host nation Japan, taking gold and bronze in the women's street event with composed performances when it mattered most. 21-year-old Sun Sibei made history by winning China's first gold in the cycling BMX freestyle, which made its Asian Games debut. "I hope this niche sport can reach a wider audience, so more people can see the twists and turns in the air, and more children can have the chance to try BMX at facilities close to home," Sun said. The younger athletes are telling a different story, a story of confidence, exploration and willingness to step into unfamiliar territory. To some extent, these Games left behind more than medals: they opened up a new path for Chinese sport. ■

item.title: China upholds principles, promotes dialogue at G20 trade ministers' meeting: commerce ministry
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-04
BEIJING, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- China played an active role in promoting dialogue and cooperation with other G20 members while upholding principles during the recent G20 trade ministers' meeting, the country's Ministry of Commerce said on Sunday. The ministry spokesperson made the remarks in response to a media question about the meeting, which was held on Sept. 30 and Oct. 1 in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, the United States. Members exchanged views on issues proposed by the U.S. G20 presidency, including opposing the weaponization of food, addressing overcapacity, eliminating forced labor, and adjusting the Most-Favored-Nation (MFN) principle. Members reached a joint statement opposing the weaponization of food, while no outcome documents were issued on the remaining matters, according to the ministry. During the meeting, the Chinese side consistently upheld an attitude of openness and cooperation, constructively participated in discussions and maintained close communication with other members, fully playing its role in promoting dialogue and cooperation, said the spokesperson. At the same time, China adhered to its principles, resolutely safeguarded the common interests of China and other developing countries, and worked to promote unity and cooperation within the G20, the ministry added. Regarding the food issue, many emerging market and developing members, including China, put forward the view that food-importing and food-exporting countries should jointly safeguard the stability of food supply chains, and that all parties have the right to take measures for domestic public policy objectives and to safeguard food security, the spokesperson said. The presidency gave positive consideration to these views, which were also fully reflected in the joint statement, the spokesperson said, adding that the outcome was the result of consensus-building and the joint efforts of all G20 members. Issues such as overcapacity and forced labor were highly controversial from the outset, said the ministry. The ministry said that at present, G20 members are generally subject to additional Section 301 tariffs under the pretext of so-called "forced labor" and are mostly targets of Section 301 investigations over the so-called "overcapacity" issue. Against this backdrop, many members put forward different views on the issues set by the presidency, and the meeting ultimately failed to produce outcome documents on these matters, the ministry said. The spokesperson also noted that, after the meeting, the U.S. side issued a chair's statement mentioning that it had released a statement on forced labor with two other G20 countries outside the G20 framework. On the issue of reforming the MFN treatment principle, the vast majority of members, including China, emphasized that the principle is the cornerstone of the multilateral trading system, providing stability and predictability for global trade, and that any undermining of this principle would seriously damage the foundation of the multilateral trading system, said the ministry. In light of the views expressed by the members, the presidency did not propose an outcome document on this topic, the ministry revealed. Looking ahead to the G20 Leaders' Summit in December 2026, the spokesperson said that China is ready to work with the G20 presidency and all members to uphold consensus-building, and jointly contribute positive and practical economic and trade outcomes to the summit. ■

item.title: China's holiday consumption market posts steady growth
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-04
BEIJING, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- Consumer spending across China is holding steady midway through the seven-day National Day holiday, with early data pointing to stable growth that reflects the economy's underlying vitality. In the first three days of the holiday from Oct. 1 to 3, foot traffic and revenue at 78 major shopping streets and commercial districts monitored by the Ministry of Commerce rose 3.4 percent and 5.3 percent year on year, respectively. Notably, the government's consumer goods trade-in program drove 19.63 billion yuan (about 2.91 billion U.S. dollars) in sales over the same period, benefiting 3.48 million consumers. In breakdown, the program drove trade-ins of 46,000 vehicles, generating 7.45 billion yuan in new car sales, along with 1.51 million home appliances worth 6.5 billion yuan and 1.71 million digital and smart devices worth 4.9 billion yuan. The National Day holiday has long been one of China's peak periods for travel, tourism and spending. Authorities had projected 2.13 billion cross-regional passenger trips in total over the seven days, averaging 300 million a day. Previous data have suggested demand remains strong as railway passenger trips on Oct. 1 alone reached 25.2 million, a single-day record. To meet surging demand, China has added train services on busy routes and waived highway tolls for private cars during the holiday. Moreover, the Ministry of Culture and Tourism launched a month-long national tourism promotion campaign in late September. Local governments are hosting more than 20,000 events spanning scenic trips, autumn outings, red tourism, study tours, night activities and local food to boost diverse premium tourism offerings, while also handing out some 310 million yuan in consumer vouchers and subsidies over the month as a way to spur tourism consumption. ■

item.title: Over 300 artifacts, documents debut in Beijing as China marks 90th anniversary of Long March victory
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-04
BEIJING, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- More than 300 artifacts and historical documents related to the Long March are being exhibited for the first time at a military museum in Beijing, offering new details about an event that helped shape the history of the 20th century. The exhibition comes as China marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March, which concluded in October 1936 when the main forces of the Red Army broke through the siege of the Kuomintang forces and reunited in northwest China. The military odyssey of roughly 12,500 kilometers, which started in 1934, not only preserved the revolutionary forces, but also gave the Communist Party of China (CPC) a new foothold from which to grow the strength of the revolution, and a new starting point from which to carry the revolution forward to victory. One highlight of the exhibition is a collection of manuscripts recounting battles, radio communications, daily experiences and other aspects of the journey. Some were written by the individuals themselves, while most were compiled from their oral accounts. These manuscripts offer valuable firsthand records, while also displaying literary merit, said a guide at the Military Museum of the Chinese People's Revolution, which is hosting the themed exhibition. Among them is a manuscript by a division commander, recounting how his unit tried to hold back enemy forces at the Xiangjiang River in late 1934. Historical records show that the Central Red Army emerged from the campaign with just over 30,000 troops, down from more than 86,000 at the start of the Long March. An exhibition curator at the museum said that the newly displayed materials, along with the personal belongings of those who died in battle, help broaden knowledge of what happened in key battles during the Long March. They also provide valuable source material for research into military history. Over the past nine decades, the Long March has drawn journalists, writers and scholars from around the world to retrace its route and explore its history as a way to understand the CPC and China today. More than a strategic military maneuver, it is widely regarded as a saga of ideals, devotion, willpower and bravery. Another group of newly displayed artifacts offers a glimpse into how Red Army soldiers pushed the limits of human endurance in some of the most unforgiving terrain along the route. They include a blue, single-layer coat and a simple knitted blanket used by soldiers to keep warm while crossing snow-covered mountains, as well as everyday items such as a fire-starting tool and a first-aid pouch. According to information presented at the exhibition, the main forces of the Red Army climbed more than 20 snow-covered mountains rising above 4,000 meters during the Long March. Thin air, deep ravines and rapidly changing weather made the journey a constant test of endurance. Some soldiers collapsed from exhaustion, while others froze to death. Hundreds of kilometers of marshland posed another formidable challenge for the Red Army. The terrain was so treacherous that it was described as a "death trap," with hidden marshes that could swallow people and animals without warning. Many soldiers lost their lives there. Some died of illness or starvation, while others were poisoned by wild plants they ate in a desperate bid to survive. Others simply disappeared in the marshes. The exhibition in Beijing features newly displayed artifacts from this ordeal, including half of a belt, with the other half having been eaten by a soldier, a fishing line used by a senior officer to catch fish for food, and straw sandals reinforced with cloth that soldiers wore while crossing the marshlands. Keith Bennett, international relations consultant and vice president of the London-based 48 Group, pointed to conviction, discipline and perseverance as enduring values of the Long March, saying they continue to inspire China's modernization and its vision of multipolarity, global cooperation and shared progress. The spirit of the Long March, he said, remains a living force in contemporary China, guiding endeavors like poverty alleviation, rural revitalization, scientific innovation, ecological civilization and major national development goals. The exhibition's new displays also turn to another part of the Long March story: the people who lived along the route. The objects offer a glimpse into the ties the CPC and the Red Army sought to build with local communities. Among these items are a tablecloth that Mao Zedong gave to a member of the Miao ethnic group in Guizhou, a volleyball soldiers left behind in Sichuan, and a pair of goggles presented to a guide in Yunnan. All three provinces lie in southwest China. Other artifacts include black ramie cloth and scissors given to people in Guizhou to show gratitude for their help, as well as a porcelain bowl presented to a family in Sichuan that took in a wounded soldier and cared for him as he recovered. Elsbeth van Paridon, a Dutch sinologist who joined a group retracing the Long March this summer, said walking the route gave her a feeling similar to looking out over the beaches of Normandy and realizing what had happened there. She described the objective of the Long March as "making it all about the people." She noted that the former revolutionary sites along the route now also serve as ecological parks, becoming part of a broader tourism economy that supports local development. "That is how you see the spirit of the Long March live on," she said. The exhibition covers around 3,300 square meters and features 875 artifacts, including individual pieces and sets, along with 186 historical documents -- 1,061 items in all. It also features 357 photographs and charts and 73 artworks. Carefully designed displays recreate key episodes along the Long March, from the seizure of the Luding Bridge and the battle to break through Lazikou Pass to a meeting held in Zunyi, Guizhou, in 1935. The museum has previously staged three themed exhibitions commemorating the Long March, in 1996, 2006 and 2016. For the first time, this year's exhibition includes English-language descriptions. It will remain on display as part of the museum's permanent exhibition. ■
